stem: Calculate the radius of the 3rd orbit of the electron in hydrogen atom.
solution:
The radius of \(n^{\text{th}}\) orbit is given by \(r_n = a_0 n^2\). Thus, the radius of the third orbit \((n = 3)\) is

\(r_3 = a_0 3^2 = 9a_0 = 9 \times 0.053\ \text{nm}\)

\(= 0.477\ \text{nm}\).

stem: In a Rutherford scattering experiment, assume that an incident alpha particle (radius 1.80 fm) is moving directly toward a target gold nucleus (radius 6.23 fm). If the alpha particle stops right at the surface of the gold nucleus, how much energy did it have to start with?
solution:
Initially when the alpha particle is far away from the gold nucleus, its total energy is equal to its kinetic energy. As it comes closer to the nucleus, more and more of its kinetic energy gets converted to potential energy. By the time it reaches the surface of the nucleus, its kinetic energy is completely converted into potential energy and it stops moving. Thus, the initial kinetic energy \(K\), of the alpha particle is equal to the potential energy when it is at the surface of the nucleus, i.e., when the distance between the gold nucleus and the alpha particle is equal to the sum of the radii of the gold nucleus and alpha particle.

\(\therefore K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2e\,Ze}{(r_1 + r_2)}\), where, \(Z\) is the atomic number of gold and \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are the radii of the gold nucleus and alpha particle respectively. For gold \(Z = 79\).

\(\therefore K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2Ze^2}{(r_1 + r_2)}\)

\(= 9 \times 10^{9}\ \dfrac{2 \times 79 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{(6.23 + 1.80) \times 10^{-15}}\)

\(= 4.533 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{J} = 28.33\ \text{MeV}\)

stem: Determine the energies of the first two excited states of the electron in hydrogen atom. What are the excitation energies of the electrons in these orbits?
solution:
The energy of the electron in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) orbit is given by \(E_n = -13.6\dfrac{1}{n^2}\ \text{eV}\).

The first two excited states have \(n = 2\) and 3. Their energies are

\(E_2 = -13.6\dfrac{1}{2^2} = -3.4\ \text{eV}\) and

\(E_3 = -13.6\dfrac{1}{3^2} = -1.51\ \text{eV}\)

Excitation energy of an electron in \(n^{\text{th}}\) orbit is the difference between its energy in that orbit and the energy of the electron in its ground state, i.e. \(-13.6\ \text{eV}\). Thus, the excitation energies of the electrons in the first two excited states are \(10.2\ \text{eV}\) and \(12.09\ \text{eV}\) respectively.

stem: Calculate the wavelengths of the first three lines in Paschen series of hydrogen atom.
solution:
The wavelengths of lines in Paschen series \((n = 3)\) are given by

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{n^2} - \dfrac{1}{m^2}\right) = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{3^2} - \dfrac{1}{m^2}\right)\) \(\text{m}^{-1}\) for \(m = 4, 5, \ldots\)

For the first three lines in the series, \(m = 4\), 5 and 6. Substituting in the above formula we get,

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_1} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{3^2} - \dfrac{1}{4^2}\right)\)

\(= 1.097 \times 10^{7} \times 7/(9 \times 16)\)

\(= 0.0533 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\)

\(\lambda_1 = 1.876 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_2} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{3^2} - \dfrac{1}{5^2}\right)\)

\(= 1.097 \times 10^{7} \times 16/(9 \times 25)\)

\(= 0.078 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\)

\(\lambda_2 = 1.282 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_3} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{3^2} - \dfrac{1}{6^2}\right)\)

\(= 1.097 \times 10^{7} \times 27/(9 \times 36)\)

\(= 0.09142 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\)

\(\lambda_3 = 1.094 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}\)

subtopic: Atomic Nucleus: Constituents, Size and Forces
stem: Calculate the radius and density of \(^{70}\text{Ge}\) nucleus, given its mass to be approximately 69.924 u.
solution:
The radius of a nucleus X with mass number \(A\) is given by \(R_X = R_0 A^{\frac{1}{3}}\), where \(R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}\)

Thus, the radius of \(^{70}\text{Ge}\) is

\(R_{Ge} = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \times 70^{1/3} = 4.945 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}\).

The density is given by \(\rho = \dfrac{3m_{Ge}}{4\pi R_{Ge}^{3}}\).

\(\therefore \rho = 3 \times 69.924 \times 1.66 \times \dfrac{10^{-27}}{4\pi\left(4.95 \times 10^{-15}\right)^{3}}\)

\(= 2.292 \times 10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}\).

stem: Calculate the binding energy of \(^{7}_{3}\text{Li}\), the masses of hydrogen and lithium atoms being 1.007825 u and 7.016 u respectively.
solution:
The binding energy is given by

\(E_B = (3m_H + 4m_n - m_{Li})c^2\)

\(= (3 \times 1.007825 + 4 \times 1.00866 - 7.016) \times 931.5 = 39.23\ \text{MeV}\)

stem: Calculate the energy released in the alpha decay of \(^{238}\text{Pu}\) to \(^{234}\text{U}\), the masses involved being \(m_{Pu} = 238.04955\) u, \(m_U = 234.04095\) u and \(m_{He} = 4.002603\) u.
solution:
The decay can be written as \(^{238}\text{Pu} \rightarrow {}^{234}\text{U} + {}^{4}\text{He}\). Its \(Q\) value, i.e., the energy released is given by

\(Q = [m_{Pu} - m_U - m_{He}]c^2\)

\(= [238.04955 - 234.04095 - 4.002603]c^2\ \text{u}\)

\(= 0.005997 \times 931.5\ \text{MeV} = 5.5862\ \text{MeV}\).

stem: Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the beta particle (positron) emitted in the decay of \(^{22}_{11}\text{Na}\), given the mass of \(^{22}_{11}\text{Na} = 21.994437\) u, \(^{22}_{10}\text{Ne} = 21.991385\) u and \(m_e = 0.00055\) u.
solution:
The decay can be written as

\(^{22}_{11}\text{Na} \rightarrow {}^{22}_{10}\text{Ne} + e^{+} +\) neutrino. The energy released is

\(Q = [m_{Na} - m_{Ne} - m_e]c^2\)

\(= [21.994437 - 21.991385 - 0.00055]c^2\)

\(= 0.002502 \times 931.5\ \text{MeV} = 2.3306\ \text{MeV}\)

This is the maximum energy that the beta particle \((e^{+})\) can have, the neutrino having zero energy in that case.

subtopic: Law of Radioactive Decay, Half-Life and Average Life
stem: The half-life of a nuclear species \(^{N}\text{X}\) is 3.2 days. Calculate its (i) decay constant, (ii) average life and (iii) the activity of its sample of mass 1.5 mg.
solution:
The half-life \((T_{1/2})\) is related to the decay constant \((\lambda)\) by

\(T_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda\) giving,

\(\lambda = 0.693/T_{1/2}\)

\(= 0.693/3.2\)

\(= 0.2166\) per day

\(= 0.2166/(24 \times 3600)\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

\(= 2.507 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{s}^{-1}\).

Average life is related to decay constant by

\(\tau = 1/\lambda = 1/0.2166\) per day \(= 4.617\) days

The activity is given by \(A = \lambda N(t)\), where \(N(t)\) is the number of nuclei in the given sample. This is given by

\(N(t) = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3}/Y = 9.03 \times 10^{20}/Y\)

Here, \(Y\) is the atomic mass of nuclear species X in g per mol.

\(\therefore A = 9.03 \times 10^{20} \times 2.5 \times 10^{-6}/Y\)

\(= 2.257 \times 10^{15}/Y\)

\(= 2.257 \times 10^{15}/(Y \times 3.7 \times 10^{10})\ \text{Ci}\)

\(= 6.1 \times 10^{4}/Y\ \text{Ci}\).

subtopic: Law of Radioactive Decay, Half-Life and Average Life
stem: The activity of a radioactive sample decreased from 350 \(\text{s}^{-1}\) to 175 \(\text{s}^{-1}\) in one hour. Determine the half-life of the species.
solution:
The time dependence of activity is given by \(A(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}\), where, \(A(t)\) and \(A_0\) are the activities at time \(t\) and 0 respectively.

\(175 = 350\,e^{-\lambda 3600}\),

or, \(3600\lambda = \ln(350/175) = \ln 2 = 0.6931\)

\(\lambda = 0.6931/3600 = 1.925 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}\).

The half-life is given by \(T_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda\).

\(\therefore T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{1.925 \times 10^{-4}} = 3.6 \times 10^{3}\ s\)

subtopic: Law of Radioactive Decay, Half-Life and Average Life
stem: In an alpha decay, the daughter nucleus produced is itself unstable and undergoes further decay. If the number of parent and daughter nuclei at time \(t\) are \(N_p\) and \(N_d\) respectively and their decay constants are \(\lambda_p\) and \(\lambda_d\) respectively. What condition needs to be satisfied in order for \(N_d\) to remain constant?
solution:
The number of parent nuclei decaying between time 0 and \(dt\), for small values of \(dt\) is given by \(N_p\lambda_p dt\). This is the number of daughter nuclei produced in time \(dt\). The number of daughter nuclei decaying in the same interval is \(N_d\lambda_d dt\). For the number of daughter nuclei to remain constant, these two quantities, i.e., the number of daughter nuclei produced in time \(dt\) and the number decaying in time \(dt\) have to be equal. Thus, the required condition is given by

\(N_p\lambda_p dt = N_d\lambda_d dt\),

or, \(N_p\lambda_p = N_d\lambda_d\)

Calculate the energy released in the fusion reaction taking place inside the Sun, \(4p \rightarrow \alpha + 2e^{+} +\) neutrinos, neglecting the energy given to the neutrinos. Mass of alpha particle being 4.001506 u.
solution:
The energy released in the process, ignoring the energy taken by the neutrinos is given by

\(Q = \left[4 \times m_p - m_{\alpha} - 2 \times m_e\right]c^2\),

\(Q = \left[4 \times 1.00728 - 4.001506 - 2 \times 0.00055\right]c^2\)

\(= 0.026514 \times 931.5 = 24.70\ \text{MeV}\)
